title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and risks of using large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT, in education. The central question is how these models might support teaching and learning while also introducing new pedagogical, ethical, and operational challenges. Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the paper synthesizes emerging examples from prior literature and develops a forward-looking argument about how LLMs could be integrated responsibly into educational systems.

The paper discusses LLM-based approaches for both learners and teachers. For learners, it highlights possible uses such as generating quizzes and practice problems, supporting reading comprehension, providing explanations and summaries, assisting writing, enabling remote tutoring, and offering accessibility supports for students with disabilities. For teachers, it describes applications including lesson planning, personalized content creation, language support, professional development, assessment assistance, plagiarism detection, and automated feedback. The authors also review recent studies using models such as GPT-3, BERT, Codex, and conversational agents in contexts like language learning, computing education, medical education, chemistry, and teacher education.

The population discussed is broad and spans elementary, secondary, university, and professional education, from both student and teacher perspectives. The paper is not tied to one implementation site or intervention context; instead, it is a conceptual overview situated in the broader educational technology landscape. The authors also extend the discussion to innovative environments such as AR/VR, remote learning, and multilingual access, while emphasizing that effective adoption depends on educator expertise, curriculum design, and human oversight.

The main conclusions are that LLMs have significant potential to enhance personalization, engagement, content generation, and instructional support, but they should not be adopted uncritically. The paper stresses risks including bias, hallucinations, copyright concerns, privacy and security issues, overreliance by students or teachers, inequitable access, and difficulty distinguishing AI-generated from student-generated work. It concludes with recommendations for responsible use: build AI literacy and critical thinking, maintain human supervision, create clear governance and privacy protections, provide teacher training, and design pedagogically grounded curricula that use LLMs as complements rather than replacements for human teaching and learning.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: A dialogue-optimized large language model from OpenAI used for natural language generation, question answering, and conversational interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as an example of a large language model for education and referenced in a cited study evaluating performance on the United States Medical Licensing Exam; the paper also uses ChatGPT as a representative educational LLM in a position-paper discussion of opportunities and risks.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Large language models and generative AI systems used for text generation, feedback, assessment support, personalization, and educational content creation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a position paper synthesizing potential educational uses, risks, and prior literature on large language models in education across learners and teachers, without conducting a new empirical evaluation.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a position paper that discusses opportunities, challenges, and prior studies but does not report an original empirical evaluation, systematic review protocol, or meta-analysis. No direct outcome data from a study conducted in this paper are provided.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper makes broad claims about possible benefits and risks of large language models in education, but it does not provide empirical effect estimates from its own evaluation. As a result, impact is conceptually important but empirically unclear within this paper.
